title: Egusi Soup

ingredients.name: onion
ingredients.amount: 1 cup blended (3-5 onions), with fresh chilies

steps: Blend the ground egusi with the onion and chili mixture into a paste and set it aside.
Warm the palm oil in a large pot over medium heat for about a minute, then stir in the iru.
Pour in the stock gradually and lower the heat to a gentle simmer.
Drop small spoonfuls of egusi paste into the pot, keeping them in little balls.
Simmer 20 to 30 minutes until the balls are cooked through.
Add your cooked meat or fish, then the pumpkin leaves and waterleaf.
Cover and cook 7 to 10 minutes until the leaves soften.
Stir in the bitter leaf and cook uncovered another 5 to 10 minutes.
Taste and adjust the salt and crayfish before serving.
story: A thick melon-seed soup cooked all over Nigeria, with each family and region making its own version. It's usually eaten with pounded yam or another swallow.
safety: Make sure any meat or fish added is fully cooked before it goes in.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Jerk Shrimp
steps: Pulse the onion, scallions, chilies, garlic and all the dry spices into a rough paste in a food processor.
With the processor running, drizzle in the soy sauce and vegetable oil.
Clean the shrimp, pat them dry, toss them with the jerk paste and let them sit about 5 minutes.
Cook the shrimp in the coconut oil in a large skillet over medium heat, then set them aside.
In the same pan, cook the shallots with the lemon juice for 3 to 5 minutes.
Return the shrimp, stir everything together for 1 to 2 minutes and serve right away.
story: A quick take on Jamaica's famous jerk seasoning, great as finger food or over rice.
safety: Shrimp are done when they turn pink and opaque all the way through.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Jollof Rice
steps: Blend the tomatoes, scotch bonnet and onion until smooth, then blend in the bell peppers.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat.
Add the pepper purée with all the spices, bay leaves and salt, and bring it to a boil.
Stir in the rice, cover and turn the heat down low.
Check after about 25 minutes: uncover if it's too wet, or add a cup or two of water if it's too dry.
Keep cooking until the rice is tender, about 45 minutes total.
story: A one-pot tomato rice loved across West Africa, and the subject of a friendly, long-running rivalry between Ghana and Nigeria over who makes it best. Often linked to the origins of Louisiana jambalaya.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Pilau Rice
steps: Warm the oil in a large pot over medium heat.
Toss in the rice and onion and stir until the rice turns from translucent to white.
Stir in the garlic, ginger and pilau masala until the garlic is cooked.
Mix the coconut milk with half a cup of broth and pour it over the rice.
Cover, turn the heat to its lowest setting, and add broth half a cup at a time until the rice is tender.
story: A fragrant spiced rice from the Swahili coast and Zanzibar, shaped by centuries of trade with India.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Chapati
steps: Dissolve the salt in 1 1/2 cups warm water with 3 tablespoons of oil.
Mix it into the flour, adding the rest of the water until the dough is soft.
Knead 10 to 15 minutes, then divide into 11 to 15 balls and cover them.
Roll each ball very thin, brush with oil, then roll it up from one edge into a coil.
Heat a non-stick pan until a drop of water sizzles away instantly.
Cook each chapati about a minute until golden underneath, flip, brush with oil, and repeat on the other side.
Stack the finished chapatis under foil to keep them soft.
story: A soft pan-fried flatbread eaten all over East Africa with stews and beans. Unlike Indian chapati, this version uses regular white flour.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Curry Potatoes
steps: Par-boil the potato cubes in salted water for about 4 minutes, then drain and rinse.
Soften the onion in the oil over medium heat for 6 to 8 minutes, then add the garlic briefly.
Stir in the spices, then the tomato paste and lemon juice.
Add the potatoes, a little salt and the water.
Cook uncovered about 10 minutes, until the potatoes are tender and the sauce coats them.
Stir in the parsley at the end and serve hot.
story: An easy, gently spiced Ugandan side that pairs well with grilled chicken or a meat stew.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Mofongo
steps: Soak the sliced plantains in salted water for 15 to 30 minutes, then drain and dry them.
Fry them in batches in the oil over medium heat for 10 to 12 minutes, until cooked but not browned.
Mash the plantains with the garlic and a splash of oil until fairly smooth.
Mix in the cracklings and salt.
Shape into balls or a mound and serve warm.
story: An Afro-Puerto Rican dish of mashed fried green plantains, traditionally pounded and sometimes served in the mortar itself.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Atakilt Wat
steps: Chop the cabbage, slice the onion and carrots, and cube the potatoes.
Heat the oil in a large pot and cook the onion and carrots for 5 minutes.
Stir in the cumin, turmeric and curry powder for a minute.
Add the water, then the potatoes and cabbage, and season.
Cover and cook on low-medium about 25 minutes, until the potatoes and cabbage are tender.
Let it rest a few minutes, then adjust the seasoning.
story: A cheap, colorful vegetable stew that's a staple of Ethiopian fasting days, served alongside other dishes on injera.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Lentil Sambusa
steps: Boil the soaked lentils about 20 minutes until tender, then drain.
Sauté the onion, garlic and jalapeño in olive oil for about 5 minutes, then add the spices for 2 minutes.
Add the lentils, cook 10 minutes, season, and let the filling cool before stirring in the cilantro.
Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C).
Place a spoonful of filling on each wrapper, wet the edges, fold into a triangle and pinch closed.
Brush with olive oil and bake 6 to 10 minutes, then flip and bake 2 to 3 minutes more.
story: Crispy lentil-filled triangles, Ethiopia's cousin of the samosa, often served during celebrations and fasting periods.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Moin Moin
steps: Pulse the soaked beans with warm water to split them, then rinse repeatedly to wash off the skins.
Blend the peeled beans with the bell pepper, onion, chili and a cup of water until very smooth.
Stir in the raw eggs, then the palm oil, crayfish, bouillon and salt dissolved in a little hot water.
Whip the mixture for about 10 minutes to make it light, and adjust the seasoning.
Pour half into an oiled loaf pan, add the sliced boiled eggs, then the rest of the mixture, and cover with foil.
Steam the pan in a covered pot of simmering water for 45 to 60 minutes until set.
story: A steamed bean pudding that's a must at Nigerian parties, often served next to jollof rice and fried plantains.
safety: It's done when a knife inserted in the center comes out clean, since it contains raw egg.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Moroccan Lentil Salad
steps: Rinse the lentils and pick out any stones.
Stud half the onion with the cloves and simmer it with the lentils in the water for about 20 minutes, until tender.
Remove the onion, drain the lentils and let them cool a little.
Whisk the lemon juice, oil, mint, cumin, coriander, garlic and salt, then toss with the lentils.
Add the other half of the onion, finely chopped, and the roasted pepper.
Chill at least 30 minutes and serve cold or at room temperature.
story: A bright, protein-rich lentil salad in the spirit of North African mezze.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Mafé

ingredients.name: beef
ingredients.amount: 2 lbs stew meat (or lamb or chicken)

steps: Whisk the peanut butter into the stock and set aside.
Season the meat and brown it in batches in the oil over medium heat, then set it aside.
Cook the onion, garlic, peppers and carrots in the same pan until the onion softens.
Pour in the peanut stock, return the meat, and add the tomatoes, thyme and bay leaf.
Bring to a boil, then simmer on low for about an hour, stirring often, until the meat is tender.
Remove the thyme and bay leaf, adjust the seasoning, and serve over rice.
story: A rich peanut and tomato stew from Senegal and Mali, with versions cooked all across West Africa.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Curry Goat
steps: Blend the curry powder, onions, scallions, chilies, ginger, garlic, thyme, salt and pepper with half a cup of water.
Rub the paste into the meat and refrigerate overnight.
Scrape the marinade off and keep it, then brown the meat gently in butter.
Move the meat to a pot with the potatoes, carrots and saved marinade, and add water to cover.
Bring to a boil, then simmer 1 to 1 1/2 hours until the meat is tender.
story: A Jamaican party classic, milder than many other curries, almost always served with rice and often fried plantains.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Waakye

ingredients.name: beans
ingredients.amount: 1 cup red beans or black-eyed peas

steps: Drain the soaked beans and boil them in a large pot of water for about 45 minutes.
Add the washed, cut sorghum leaves for about 5 minutes to color the beans, then remove them. Use baking soda if you can't find the leaves.
Add the washed rice and more water.
Cook 15 to 20 minutes, stirring so nothing burns, until the rice and beans are tender and the water is absorbed.
Season with salt and serve with stew, egg, fish or meat.
story: A rice-and-beans dish from northern Ghana, colored reddish-brown by sorghum leaves and sold everywhere as a breakfast and lunch favorite.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Suya
steps: Soak wooden skewers in water for 20 minutes and heat the oven to 450°F (230°C).
Mix all the spices and bouillon, then add the peanuts, crushed into a fine powder but not a paste.
Pat the steak dry and slice it thinly on the diagonal.
Thread the slices onto skewers and coat both sides with the spice mix.
Drizzle with oil and bake 12 to 15 minutes, switching to broil for the last few minutes for a crisp outside.
story: Spicy grilled beef skewers first made by Hausa cooks in northern Nigeria and neighboring countries, now a beloved street food across Nigeria.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Peri Peri Chicken
advance_prep: Marinate at least 3 hours, ideally overnight.
steps: Whisk everything except the chicken into a marinade, coat the chicken, cover and refrigerate.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) and get an oven-safe skillet very hot on the stove.
Sear the chicken 2 to 3 minutes per side until browned, keeping the marinade.
Pour the marinade over the chicken and move the skillet into the oven.
Bake 15 to 20 minutes, until cooked through.
story: Named after the fiery African bird's-eye chili, this dish grew from Portuguese and southern African cooking traditions meeting in Mozambique and South Africa.
safety: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) inside. Boil the used marinade before serving it as a sauce.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Braised Lamb Shank with Couscous
steps: Heat the oven to 325°F (160°C). Season the shanks and brown them two at a time in half the oil, about 12 minutes.
In the rest of the oil, cook the onion, carrots and garlic about 5 minutes, then toast the spices for a minute.
Stir in the tomato paste and harissa for 2 minutes, then add the wine and reduce to a thick syrup.
Add the tomatoes and 1 cup of broth, bring to a boil, and nestle in the lamb.
Cover and braise in the oven about 3 hours, basting now and then, until the meat nearly falls off the bone.
Toast the almonds, then reduce the strained sauce on the stove and return the lamb and vegetables to it.
For the couscous, soften the shallot in butter, toast the couscous briefly, add the remaining broth, water and salt, boil, then add currants, cover off the heat for 10 minutes and fluff.
Mix the herbs with the almonds, stir half into the couscous, and serve the lamb and sauce around it with the rest on top.
story: A slow-braised, sweet-and-spicy lamb dish in the style of Moroccan celebration cooking.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Key Wat (Spicy Beef Stew)
steps: Season the beef and brown it in batches in half the oil in a heavy pot, then set it aside.
Add the rest of the oil, lower the heat, and cook the onion slowly until golden, about 15 minutes.
Add the garlic for a minute, then the tomato paste, berbere and sugar, and cook into a thick paste.
Pour in the stock, return the beef, bring to a boil, then simmer 1 to 2 hours.
Shred the beef with two forks, return it to the pot, and simmer 15 minutes more.
story: A deep red Ethiopian stew built on berbere, the country's signature chili spice blend, and eaten with injera.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Jerk Chicken

ingredients.name: chicken
ingredients.amount: legs and thighs from two 3.5-4 lb chickens

steps: Process the onion, scallions, chilies, garlic and spices into a coarse paste, then blend in the soy sauce and oil.
Coat the chicken in the marinade and refrigerate overnight.
Let the chicken come to room temperature.
Grill over medium-high heat, turning now and then, for 35 to 40 minutes until well browned and cooked through. Cover the grill for a smokier taste.
story: Jerk is Jamaica's signature way of cooking with a fiery allspice and scotch bonnet marinade, and it has traveled with the Caribbean diaspora around the world.
safety: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) at the thickest part.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Chermoula Fish
steps: Blend the oil, garlic, cilantro, lemon juice and spices into a smooth chermoula.
Coat the fish with about half a cup of it and refrigerate.
Cook the grated carrots and potatoes with the rest of the chermoula in a covered skillet for 25 to 30 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C). Shape the vegetables into 4 nests on a baking sheet and set a fillet on each.
Top with chopped bell pepper, chopped preserved lemon rind and cherry tomatoes, cover with foil, and bake 12 to 17 minutes.
story: Chermoula is Morocco's classic herb and spice marinade for fish, especially along its coasts.
safety: Fish is done at 145°F (63°C), when it flakes easily.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Rum Cake
advance_prep: Soak the dried fruit in wine and rum at least a day ahead.
steps: Mix the flour with the baking powder, spices and salt, then stir in the breadcrumbs and lime rind.
Cream the butter and sugar in a big bowl and add the browning.
Stir in about 4 cups of the soaked fruit.
Whisk the eggs until very frothy, add the rose water, sherry and vanilla, and fold into the butter mixture.
Gradually fold in the flour mixture. The batter should be thick enough to hold a spoon upright.
Pour into greased, lined tins and bake about 2 hours at 300°F (150°C), with a pan of water on the oven floor to keep it moist.
story: A dark, fruit-soaked cake that's a centerpiece of Jamaican Christmas and weddings.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Kelewele
steps: Mix the grated ginger, pepper and salt into the water.
Cut the plantains into bite-size cubes and toss them in the spice mix.
Heat oil deep enough for the plantains to float, to about 350°F (175°C).
Fry in small batches, turning once, until golden on both sides.
Drain on paper towels and keep warm while you fry the rest.
story: Spicy-sweet fried plantain cubes sold by Ghanaian street vendors, especially in the evenings.
safety: Keep the batches small so the oil doesn't bubble over.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Puff Puff
steps: Stir the salt, sugar and yeast into the warm water and wait 5 minutes.
Mix in the flour and let the batter rise 1 to 2 hours.
Heat at least 3 inches of oil. Test with a drop of batter: it should float up quickly.
Drop in spoonfuls of batter and fry a few minutes per side until golden.
Drain on paper towels and roll in sugar if you like.
story: Fluffy fried dough balls that are a fixture of Nigerian parties and street snacks.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Festival Dumplings
steps: Whisk the flour, baking powder, cornmeal, sugar and salt together.
Add the vanilla and water a little at a time, then knead 5 to 7 minutes into a firm, slightly sticky dough.
Cover and rest about 30 minutes.
Divide into 8 pieces and shape into thin logs or small balls.
Fry in medium-hot oil 5 to 6 minutes, turning halfway, then drain.
story: Slightly sweet fried cornmeal dumplings, a Jamaican beach food traditionally eaten with escovitch fish or jerk.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)

title: Mandazi
steps: Bring the ingredients to room temperature and mix them into a soft, non-sticky dough.
Roll it out about a quarter inch thick and cut into triangles.
Fry in hot oil until golden on both sides.
Drain on paper towels and serve warm. Try adding cardamom, coconut or a dusting of sugar.
story: Lightly sweet East African doughnuts, often shaped into triangles and eaten with tea for breakfast.
source: Demand Africa, At One with Food (www.demandafrica.com)
